conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this awful stomach pain for three days. It’s in my upper belly and goes to my back. I can’t eat, I’ve been throwing up, and I just feel so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, low-grade fevers—around 100 to 101. And night sweats. I’m also worried my GJ tube site might be infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We checked your blood sugar in the ER—it was very high, 764. And your labs show some acid buildup, which suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my urine didn’t show ketones. Does that mean it’s not DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Sometimes with poor blood flow or dehydration, ketones don’t show up in urine even if DKA is starting. Your blood work still shows signs of it, so we’re treating it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids and insulin to bring your sugar down safely. We’ll also keep an eye on your electrolytes and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has come down to 433 after the first insulin dose. That’s improving. We’ll keep adjusting the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because I haven’t been eating? I haven’t taken my insulin either—I just didn’t feel like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Not eating and skipping insulin can throw your sugars way off, even without infection. We’ll work with the diabetes team to adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My port hurts when they try to flush it. It’s been burning for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order an X-ray to check if there’s a kink or blockage. That could explain the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows a possible kink in the catheter near your collarbone. We’re going to do a port study to check the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some pressure, but we’ll go slow. The radiologist will explain everything before starting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port study didn’t show a leak, but you had severe pain during the flush. The X-ray suggests pinch-off syndrome—where the catheter gets compressed between bones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why it hurts? What can we do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend removing the old port and putting in a new one on the other side. A double-lumen port will give us better access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s done under general anesthesia. The surgery team will take care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is still high this morning—403. We’re increasing your insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky sometimes. Is that the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re watching closely. Your levels are coming down steadily, which is good. We’ll keep adjusting to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My magnesium was low yesterday. Did you fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave you supplements. Your latest level is better, but still a bit low. We’ll keep giving it through the IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anion gap has closed, and your bicarbonate is normal. That means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that part is under control. Now we’re focusing on your port surgery and making sure your pain is managed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the surgery tomorrow. Will I be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is routine. You’ll be asleep, and the team does this often. The old port is causing pain, so replacing it should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went perfectly. We removed the old port from your right side and placed a new double-lumen one in your left neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts a little, but not like before. Is it safe to use already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both chambers are working. We’ll start using it for meds and labs. You should feel much better with the new one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My calcium dropped today. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s low, but we’re giving you supplements. It’s likely related to your chronic pancreatitis and nutrition. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Blood sugar is stable, electrolytes are improving, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure your pain is controlled and you’re comfortable with your insulin again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to get my pain meds renewed soon. Will you give me a new prescription?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on your regular pain meds here, but we won’t give a new prescription. Your contract is with your PCP, and they’ll handle the renewal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my albuterol more. I feel a little short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are normal, and lungs are clear. It might be from anxiety or pain. Keep using your inhaler as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to change my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The diabetes team adjusted your sliding scale. We’ll give you a sheet to take home with the new instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel better, but I was worried about the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new port is working well. Just keep the site clean and let your doctor know if it becomes red or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I don’t want another DKA episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your glargine at bedtime and use the sliding scale with meals. Eat regularly—even if you’re not hungry—and don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual hydrocodone and ibuprofen as prescribed. Your PCP will handle the refill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the port? Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting for a few days. Otherwise, you can use it normally. The nurse will go over care before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You did well. Just follow up with your doctors and call if your sugar goes too high or low, or if you have pain with the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I stop smoking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It would help your diabetes and overall health. We can give you resources if you’re ready to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. Let your PCP know—they can support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. The nurse will bring them shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Goodbye.
